aiPrompt.systemPrompt: You are a master middle school math teacher.
aiPrompt.mainPrompt: Below is a student's mathematics document, as a text summary, a picture, or both. Either may be absent. Evaluate and categorize it.
aiPrompt.categorizationDescription: Categorize the document based on its content and the general proportional reasoning curriculum found in middle grades mathematics.
aiPrompt.keyIndicatorsPrompt: Return exactly one item: a single sentence of at most 30 words, written to the student as "you", saying why this category fits by naming one specific thing in their document - a number, ratio, label, table column, or phrase they actually wrote. Do not restate the problem, summarize the document as a whole, or explain the mathematics in general.

aiUnitSummary.overview: Variables and Patterns is a grade 7 introduction to algebraic relationships, framed by a student company planning a bike tour. Investigation 1 establishes what a variable is and how a relationship between two of them can be told as a story, recorded in a table and drawn as a graph — starting with a jumping-jack experiment where performance falls off with fatigue, then following the tour day by day, including what a graph can and cannot say about what happened between two recorded points. Investigation 2 moves beyond time as the independent variable to rental costs, ticket prices and the relationship between price and number of customers, which decreases rather than increases, and practises reading the story out of a graph. Investigation 3 adds equations as a fourth representation, deriving them from patterns in a table, and compares equation, table, graph and guess-and-check as strategies for the same question.

entries.priorKnowledge: From Comparing Quantities and earlier work: ratio and rate; reading and building a table; plotting points on a coordinate grid; describing a pattern in words. The terms variable, independent and dependent variable are introduced in this unit rather than assumed.
entries.problemDigest: Opens the unit with an experiment producing data that is not neatly linear. Students perform jumping jacks over a period and record the count against elapsed time, so the rate falls off as they tire and the pattern is theirs rather than given. The What If section supplies several groups' descriptions and tables and asks students to match each description to its table and explain how they decided — so reading a pattern of change out of a table, and recognising it from a verbal story, is the work. This establishes the unit's central move of treating a story, a table and later a graph as three accounts of one relationship.
entries.approachGuidance: Students generate their own data, which will differ between groups and will not be smooth. Work from what a group actually recorded.

entries.priorKnowledge: Variables and the idea that one may depend on another; recording a relationship in a table; reading a pattern of change out of a table and matching it to a verbal description; plotting points on a coordinate grid.
entries.problemDigest: Adds the graph as a third representation of the same relationship. Students graph the jumping-jack data from the previous problem and then, in the What If section, match graphs produced by several groups to the tables and descriptions already matched in 1.1, explaining how they decided each. Because the underlying data is the students' own, the graphs show real irregularity rather than a tidy curve. The problem establishes how the shape of a graph corresponds to a pattern of change described in words or seen in a table, which is the skill the rest of the unit depends on.
entries.approachGuidance: Matching rests on reasoning about shape rather than computation, and more than one justification can be sound. Support the student's explanation of how they matched.

entries.priorKnowledge: Variables, tables and graphs as accounts of one relationship; reading a pattern of change from any of them; time as an independent variable; rate, distance and time, and that distance accumulates over time.
entries.problemDigest: Follows the tour partners testing their route and introduces a subtle point about graphs. Students work with time and distance data for a day's ride, building the table and graph and describing the pattern — including stops and changes of pace. The What If section is the heart of the problem: Malcolm wonders what happened between two recorded points, (4.5, 40) and (5.0, 45), and five different travel stories are offered, each matching a different path between those points. Students match each story to its graph, which makes explicit that a graph records the points measured and that connecting them involves an assumption.
entries.approachGuidance: Several different journeys fit the same two recorded points, and that ambiguity is the lesson. Support the story a student attaches to a path rather than a single reading.

entries.priorKnowledge: Time, rate and distance related in tables and graphs; that a graph between recorded points involves assumptions; reading a pattern of change; constructing a table and graph from a description.
entries.problemDigest: Reverses the direction: students are given notes about a day's travel rather than data, and must identify the variables, build their own table and graph, and say how each shows the pattern of change. Because the notes are incomplete, students' tables and graphs legitimately differ, and the problem asks directly whether theirs match their classmates' and why not. The What If section adds a complication — the group must double back to retrieve a forgotten backpack — which makes distance from the start decrease for a stretch, so the graph is no longer increasing throughout.
entries.approachGuidance: The notes under-determine the data, so tables and graphs will differ between students by design. Support a representation consistent with the story rather than one answer.

entries.priorKnowledge: Variables, tables and graphs; independent and dependent variables; reading values and patterns from a table or graph; rates and unit rates; that a relationship can be read in either direction.
entries.problemDigest: Moves the independent variable away from time. Two bike shops quote rental costs differently — one given as a table, the other as a graph — and students must compare them to choose a supplier. The What If section works through Sarah's questions, which require reading each representation in both directions: the cost for 20, 40 and 32 bikes, and the number of bikes affordable on budgets of $900 and $400, which means entering the table or graph from the dependent side. Students then compare the patterns in the two representations and find the cost of a single bike from each.
entries.approachGuidance: One supplier is given as a table and the other as a graph, so comparison requires a choice of method. Support the student's route rather than converting both to one form.

entries.priorKnowledge: Independent and dependent variables and that the choice depends on the question; reading tables and graphs; income, expenses and profit; that a relationship may increase or decrease.
entries.problemDigest: Introduces a decreasing relationship and the idea of profit. The partners must set a ticket price low enough to attract customers but high enough that income exceeds expenses, so the independent variable is price and the dependent variable is the number of people — and raising one lowers the other, unlike every relationship so far. Students analyse the data and examine Malcolm's graph and the claim he makes from it. The closing discussion draws the contrast explicitly with the time-and-distance relationships of Investigation 1, and connects the shape of this graph to one seen earlier.
entries.approachGuidance: Choosing a price involves weighing income against expenses, with a range of defensible answers. Support the reasoning rather than identifying an optimum.

entries.priorKnowledge: Independent and dependent variables; increasing and decreasing relationships; reading a pattern of change from a graph; that the shape of a graph describes how two variables are related.
entries.problemDigest: Focuses entirely on reading the story out of a graph. The problem sets out the questions to ask of any graph or table — what the variables are, whether one depends on the other, and what the shape says about the relationship. The What If section gives several descriptions of things that change over time and, for each, has students decide which variable is dependent, describe the relationship, and find the graph that represents it — or sketch a new graph if none of those offered fits, which is what stops the task being pure matching. The emphasis is qualitative throughout, with no values to compute.
entries.approachGuidance: Students may need to sketch a graph where none fits, and shapes can be defended in more than one way. Support the sketch and the reasoning behind it.

entries.priorKnowledge: Variables, tables and graphs; independent and dependent variables; time, rate and distance; reading patterns of change; that a constant rate gives a steady change in a table.
entries.problemDigest: Introduces equations as a fourth representation, derived from a pattern already in a table. The group drives 320 miles home, and students estimate the travel time at 40, 50 and 60 miles per hour, using Malcolm's strategy of reading the pattern in a table and writing an equation from it. Because the distance is fixed, time falls as speed rises — so the relationship is again decreasing, and is not linear. The problem's work is moving from a pattern observed in a table to a general statement that covers any speed, which is the step from arithmetic to algebra in this unit.
entries.approachGuidance: The equation is meant to emerge from a pattern a student finds in their own table. Support that derivation rather than supplying the relationship.

entries.priorKnowledge: Equations written from patterns in a table; tables, graphs and verbal descriptions of a relationship; independent and dependent variables; that one question can be answered from any representation.
entries.problemDigest: Compares strategies directly. A $50 discount is applied to the tour price and students must find what a customer finally pays. The What If section sets four approaches side by side — Lisa's equation, Xavier's table, Mikala's graph and Pat's guess-and-check — and asks students to describe how each would be used and, more importantly, when each makes sense, so the comparison is about fitness for purpose rather than correctness. Sidney's observation that a $50 tour would cost the customer nothing raises whether the model holds across its whole range, which is a question about the situation rather than the arithmetic.
entries.approachGuidance: Four strategies are compared for when each is appropriate, with none preferred. Support the student's choice and their reasoning about its fit.

entries.priorKnowledge: All four representations — description, table, graph and equation — and moving between them; independent and dependent variables; increasing and decreasing relationships; writing an equation from a pattern; income, expenses and profit.
entries.problemDigest: Closes the unit by planning a further tour with everything built so far. Students work across representations to answer questions about the new tour, choosing for each whether a table, graph, equation or informal reasoning is the most appropriate tool, and justifying the choice. The problem functions as a review in which selecting and moving between representations is the content rather than any single technique, and it returns to the business context of costs, prices and profit that has run through Investigations 2 and 3.
entries.approachGuidance: Each question can be answered from more than one representation and choosing is part of the task. Support the selection the student makes.

entries.priorKnowledge: The whole unit: variables and the dependence of one on another; description, table, graph and equation as four accounts of one relationship and how to move between them; increasing and decreasing patterns of change; that a graph between recorded points involves assumptions; writing an equation from a pattern in a table.
entries.problemDigest: The unit's Mathematical Reflections, asking what students know about variables and the patterns relating them. The expected ground is what a variable is and how the independent and dependent roles are decided by the question being asked; how a story, a table, a graph and an equation each show the same relationship and what each makes easy to see; how to read a pattern of change from any of them, whether increasing, decreasing or irregular; why connecting points on a graph involves an assumption about what happened in between; and when an equation, a table, a graph or guess-and-check is the appropriate tool for a question.

entries.priorKnowledge: Whatever has been covered when the exercises are assigned; the banks are organised by investigation and are normally used alongside the corresponding problems rather than after the whole unit.
entries.problemDigest: The unit's ACE question banks — Applications, Connections and Extensions — gathered as one item and grouped by investigation rather than taught as a problem. The banks follow the investigations: identifying variables and matching descriptions, tables and graphs of a changing relationship, including time-and-distance situations; reading tables and graphs in both directions, comparing two pricing or rental relationships, and working with decreasing relationships and with income, expenses and profit; and writing equations from patterns in tables, then using equations, tables, graphs or guess-and-check to answer questions and judging which suits a given question. This is the unit's largest item by a wide margin and is individual practice on content introduced elsewhere.
